title: Chiral magnons for spin-qubit state transfer
authors: Martijn Dols, Carlos Gonzalez-Ballestero, Mikhail Cherkasskii, Christian L. Degen, Victor A. S. V. Bittencourt, Silvia Viola Kusminskiy
abstract: We propose a protocol where chiral magnons mediate a state transfer between two distant spin qubits. The protocol is implemented by varying the coupling between the spin qubits and the magnons in time, such that an arbitrary state is transferred from one qubit to the other. The modulation of the coupling is performed such that the two-spin-qubit state is kept as a dark state of the magnon bath, bypassing the associated losses. We show that the protocol can be realized on a hybrid system composed of two nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers coupled to the nonreciprocal and chiral magnon modes of an yttrium iron garnet (YIG) stripe. We propose two methods to achieve the time modulation of the NV-magnon coupling: i) the NV-magnet distance of both NV centers is varied; ii) the external magnetic field and the NV-magnet distance of one NV center are varied. We evaluate the implementability of both methods numerically, including the constraints on the temperature, and the dephasing time and minimal lifetime of the spin qubits required for high-fidelity state transfer. We find that using realistic experimental parameters, a state transfer between NV centers at a distance of several microns can be achieved with a fidelity $\gtrsim 0.95$. Our findings expand the toolbox of magnonics for quantum information purposes.
summary: The authors present a protocol for transferring quantum states between two distant spin qubits mediated by chiral magnons in a YIG/NV center hybrid system. They achieve this by dynamically controlling the coupling such that decoherence losses are avoided via dark-state engineering. This work expands the utility of magnonics as a robust tool for quantum information processing at solid-state distances.
main_problem: The paper proposes a protocol to transfer an arbitrary quantum state between two distant spin qubits using chiral magnons as mediators.
main_result: High-fidelity state transfer ($\gtrsim 0.95$) can be achieved over several micron distances using realistic experimental parameters.
method: State transfer is realized by time-modulating the coupling strength such that the two-spin-qubit system remains in a dark state of the magnon bath, thereby bypassing decoherence losses.
model_or_system: The physical platform is a hybrid system combining two Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) centers coupled to nonreciprocal and chiral magnon modes within an yttrium iron garnet (YIG) stripe. The dynamics are modeled using a master equation incorporating time-dependent coupling terms.
key_observables: State transfer fidelity ($F$), which is shown to exceed 0.95 under optimal conditions.
important_parameters: The distance between NV centers (several microns), temperature, dephasing time ($T_\phi$), and spin qubit lifetime ($T_1$).
main_assumptions: The Markov approximation is used for the master equation, and it assumes that the two-spin-qubit state can be kept in a dark state relative to the magnon bath.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the Hamiltonian structure showing unidirectional effective coupling. Figure 3 demonstrates fidelity degradation as temperature increases due to thermal excitation effects.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the protocol, models the system dynamics using a master equation incorporating time-dependent couplings, details two methods for achieving this time modulation (varying distance or magnetic field), and concludes with numerical evaluations of feasibility.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses quantum networking by proposing a solid-state mechanism to mediate long-range entanglement and state transfer between qubits using magnonic excitations, which is highly relevant to open quantum systems research.

Spintronics.note: The core mechanism involves coupling quantum information (spin qubits) to magnonic modes in a YIG system, which directly falls under the scope of magnon-photon/magnon-qubit interactions central to spintronics.
